content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Debugging Running Containers (nsenter, exec)"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"When troubleshooting Docker containers, simply relying on logs is often not enough. You may need to inspect the live filesystem, network states, or running processes. This tutorial covers two primary methods for debugging running Docker containers: docker exec and nsenter."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Method 1: Using docker exec"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The docker exec command runs a new command inside a running container. This is the most common and straightforward way to debug a container interactively."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Spawns a new process inside the existing container's namespaces."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Requires a shell (like sh or bash) to be present inside the container image."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"docker exec -it <container_name_or_id> /bin/sh"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"Once inside the container shell, you can run standard diagnostic commands like ps aux, netstat, or cat /etc/resolv.conf."},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"Method 2: Using nsenter (Advanced Troubleshooting)"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"What happens if a container lacks a shell (e.g., minimal scratch images or distroless images) or if docker exec fails? You can use nsenter to enter the Linux namespaces of the container directly from the host."},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"First, find the Process ID (PID) of the target container using docker inspect:"},{"order":12,"type":"code","text":"docker inspect --format \"{{.State.Pid}}\" <container_name_or_id>"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Next, use nsenter to join all namespaces (mount, pid, net, ipc, uts) of that PID from the host machine:"},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"sudo nsenter --target <PID> --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Use docker exec for everyday debugging when a shell is available. Reserve nsenter for advanced scenarios involving stripped-down containers where low-level host access is required."}]
